questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the following:

(i) Income elasticity of demand. (5 marks)

(ii) Cross elasticity of demand. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Income elasticity of demand (YED) (5 marks)**

*Definition.* Income elasticity of demand measures the **responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in consumers' income**, the price of the good and all other factors staying constant.

$$\text{YED} = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded}}{\%\ \text{change in income}}$$

*Interpretation.*

- **YED > 1**: demand rises more than proportionately to income. The good is a **luxury** or *superior* good (for example cars, restaurant meals, air travel). Example (hypothetical): income rises by 10% and the quantity demanded rises by 20%, so YED $= 20/10 = +2$.
- **0 < YED < 1**: demand rises less than proportionately: a **necessity** or *normal* good (for example bread, salt, soap).
- **YED < 0**: demand **falls** when income rises: an **inferior good** (for example cheap second-hand clothes, low-quality cassava flour in place of rice). Example (hypothetical): income rises by 10% and the quantity demanded falls by 6%, so YED $= -6/10 = -0.6$.
- **YED = 0**: demand does not depend on income.

*Uses.* Firms use YED to forecast the effect of growth or recession on their sales and to decide which products to expand; governments use it for taxation, development planning and the study of changes in the structure of the economy (as income grows, the share of food falls and that of manufactures and services rises).

**(ii) Cross elasticity of demand (XED) (5 marks)**

*Definition.* Cross elasticity of demand measures the **responsiveness of the quantity demanded of one good (A) to a change in the price of another good (B)**.

$$\text{XED} = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded of good A}}{\%\ \text{change in price of good B}}$$

*Interpretation.*

- **Substitutes** (goods that can replace each other): XED is **positive**, because a higher price of B makes buyers switch to A. Example (hypothetical): the price of coffee rises by 10% and the quantity of tea demanded rises by 5%, so XED $= +5/10 = +0.5$. The higher the value, the closer the substitutes.
- **Complements** (goods used together): XED is **negative**, because a higher price of B reduces the demand for A as well. Example (hypothetical): the price of petrol rises by 10% and the demand for cars falls by 15%, so XED $= -15/10 = -1.5$.
- **Unrelated goods**: XED is **zero** (or close to zero).

*Uses.* Firms use XED to see how rivals' price changes affect them and to define the boundaries of a market (goods with a high positive XED are in the same market); governments and competition authorities use it to judge market power.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What factors determine the price elasticity of demand?

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures the responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in its own price:

$$\text{PED} = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}$$

Demand is **elastic** if the absolute value of PED is greater than 1 and **inelastic** if it is less than 1. The main determinants are the following.

1. **Availability and closeness of substitutes.** The more numerous and the closer the substitutes, the more elastic the demand, because consumers can switch easily when the price rises (for example one brand of soap or one brand of mobile credit against another). Goods with no close substitute, such as salt or electricity for lighting, have inelastic demand.
2. **Nature of the good: necessity or luxury.** Necessities (basic food, medicine, cooking fuel) have inelastic demand because they must be bought whatever the price; luxuries (jewellery, foreign holidays, large cars) have elastic demand.
3. **Proportion of income spent on the good.** If the good takes a **small** share of income (matches, salt), a price rise is hardly noticed and demand is inelastic; if it takes a **large** share (housing, a car), a price change matters and demand is more elastic.
4. **Time period.** Demand is more inelastic in the **short run** and more elastic in the **long run**, because consumers need time to find substitutes, change habits or change equipment (for example moving from petrol to gas-powered vehicles).
5. **Definition of the good (broad or narrow).** A narrowly defined good (one brand of tea) has many substitutes and an elastic demand; a broadly defined good (food, tea in general) has fewer and a more inelastic demand.
6. **Habit, addiction and brand loyalty.** Goods bought out of habit or addiction (cigarettes, alcohol) or because of strong loyalty to a brand have inelastic demand.
7. **Durability and possibility of postponing purchase.** If the purchase can be delayed or the old good repaired (furniture, clothes, a vehicle), demand is more elastic; goods that must be bought now (medicines in an emergency) are inelastic.
8. **Range of uses (joint demand).** A good with many uses (electricity, wood) has a more elastic demand in total, because consumers can cut some uses when the price rises; the good needed with another one (a spare part for a machine already bought) has an inelastic demand.
9. **Level of price and income of the consumer.** At a very high price consumers become more price-sensitive; for high-income consumers a price change matters less.

**Conclusion.** The size of the PED depends mostly on substitutes, on whether the good is a necessity, on its weight in the budget and on the time allowed; knowing it helps firms to set prices (raising the price of an inelastic good increases revenue) and helps the government to choose which goods to tax.
